Incontinence means the inability to control something that should be under your control — most often, your own body's release of waste, but sometimes your own emotions or impulses. Think of it as a breakdown of the "hold it in" mechanism, whether physical or behavioural.
Meaning 1 — The Medical Sense (Most Common Today)

This is by far the most widely used meaning. In medicine, incontinence refers to the inability to control when urine or faeces leaves the body. In other words, the body releases waste at unintended, involuntary moments — not when the person chooses, but when the body simply can't hold it any longer.

A person experiencing incontinence does not do this on purpose. Their muscles or nerves responsible for "holding things in" are weakened, damaged, or not functioning properly, so waste escapes without warning or against their will.

The two types by what is lost:

  • Urinary incontinence — the accidental or uncontrolled leaking of urine (pee). This is the most commonly talked-about type. For example, some people leak urine when they sneeze, laugh, or cough. Others feel a sudden, overwhelming urge to urinate but cannot make it to a bathroom in time.
  • Faecal incontinence (also called bowel incontinence) — the inability to control when stool (faeces) passes out of the body. This is less discussed publicly but equally real and medically significant.

Who does it affect?

Incontinence can affect anyone, but it is especially common in:

  • Older adults, because muscles weaken with age
  • Women who have given birth, as childbirth can weaken pelvic floor muscles
  • People with certain medical conditions such as diabetes, multiple sclerosis, or prostate problems
  • People who have suffered nerve damage or spinal cord injuries

It is not a normal part of ageing that simply must be accepted — it is a medical condition that can often be treated or managed.

Important note on dignity

Incontinence is a medical issue, not a personal failing or something to be ashamed of. Millions of people worldwide live with it. Medically, it is taken seriously because it can significantly affect a person's quality of life, confidence, and independence.
Meaning 2 — The Formal or Literary Sense (Older, Less Common Today)

Before the medical meaning became dominant, incontinence was widely used to describe a lack of self-restraint or self-control over one's desires, behaviour, or impulses — particularly around physical pleasures like food, drink, or sexual desire.

Think of it this way: just as the body in the medical sense cannot "hold back" waste, a person in this figurative sense cannot "hold back" their urges or impulses. They act on every craving immediately, without discipline or moderation.

For example:

  • A person who eats compulsively with no self-control might be described as showing incontinence of appetite.
  • In older texts, sexual incontinence referred to excessive, unrestrained sexual behaviour.
  • More broadly, any wild, uncontrolled giving-in to passion or emotion could be labelled incontinence.

You are most likely to encounter this meaning in classical literature, philosophy, religious texts, or formal writing. In everyday modern conversation, this sense has largely faded, but it is still understood and used in educated or formal contexts.

The related adjective is incontinent, meaning "unable to control" — as in, "She became incontinent after the surgery" (medical sense), or "He was incontinent of rage" (figurative sense, meaning he could not restrain his anger).

Both meanings share one unifying idea: something that should be held in is coming out unchecked. Whether it is urine, faeces, anger, desire, or appetite — incontinence always points to a failure of control or restraint. The medical sense is about the body's physical control. The figurative sense is about the mind's or will's control. Same concept, different domain.

• "The doctor diagnosed her with urinary incontinence and recommended pelvic floor exercises."
  • "Incontinence affects millions of elderly people and is a leading reason for care home admissions."
  • "The philosopher warned that incontinence of desire — the inability to resist temptation — was the root of many moral failures."
  • "Wearing protective pads helped him manage his incontinence and maintain an active lifestyle."
Incontinence = the inability to control the release of something — in modern use, almost always the body's waste (urine or faeces); in formal or classical use, one's own impulses or desires.
